s: A sequence of local transactions where each step has a compensating undo, maintaining consistency without distributed locks.
w: Instead of one ACID transaction across services, each step commits locally and publishes an event. The next step consumes and continues. If step N fails, previously completed steps execute their compensating transactions in reverse order. Choreography sagas use events (order-created -> payment-charged -> inventory-reserved); orchestration sagas use a central coordinator telling each service what to do and when to compensate.
use: Order fulfillment spanning payment, inventory, and shipping across microservices
Any cross-service operation requiring eventual consistency without 2PC
Multi-step business processes where partial completion is acceptable
avoid: Operations requiring strict read-after-write consistency across services (use 2PC or single DB)
Simple two-step processes where a try/catch and HTTP call suffices
Workflows with no compensating action possible (impossible to undo email send)
world: Uber ride matching + payment + driver payout

pat.d: Services publish events; each listens and reacts - no central coordinator.
Central workflow engine drives steps and compensations in sequence.

pits: Compensation logic harder than forward logic - design compensations alongside forward steps
Partial failures leaving inconsistent intermediate state without proper timeout handling
tips: Choreography vs orchestration debate is the core discussion: choreography = loose coupling, orchestration = visibility
Temporal/Cadence make saga code read linearly - huge simplification over raw event choreography
